name: Code
summary: The syntax highlighting colors of code, one per category, the surface of a block of code and the states of marked lines, readable on every surface in every mode.
description: Code samples, token paths and snippets are set in the mono family (Typography foundation); this foundation colors them. Each syntax category (keyword, variable, function, class and type, string, number, comment) has a semantic color from the Figma library's code colors, global.text.code; the design system adds colors for diffs, invalid code and links, and backgrounds for marked lines, all picked from colors it already has. A block of code sits on the Figma library's code surface, global.bg.code.surface, the translucent neutral subtle fill. Everything else in code (plain identifiers, operators, punctuation) keeps the primary on-base text color. A highlighter maps the categories of its grammars to these colors: on the web, a Shiki theme generated from the tokens does it once for every mode, and a style sheet draws the marked lines.

rules.name: Categories
rules.text: Seven categories are colored: keyword (language keywords and storage modifiers, markup tag names, CSS at-rules and pseudo-classes), variable (variables, parameters, properties and object keys, CSS properties and custom properties, markup attribute names, YAML keys), function (function and method names, CSS functions), class and type (class, type and built-in object names, CSS class and id selectors), string (strings, regular expressions, markup attribute values), number (numbers and language constants such as true, null, CSS units and keywords) and comment.

rules.name: Diffs, invalid code and links
rules.text: Five more text colors cover what is not syntax: inserted, deleted and changed for the lines of a diff (green, red and orange, the success, error and severe hues), invalid for code a grammar marks invalid or deprecated (the error hue), link for URLs and links (the brand hue). They are the design system's additions to the Figma library, picked from colors it already has: the steps of the matching text roles, moved to a passing step where a role fails on a surface.

rules.name: Plain code
rules.text: What belongs to no category keeps the primary on-base text color (global.text.on-base.neutral.primary): plain identifiers a grammar does not classify, operators and punctuation. Highlighting only adds color to the structure; the code reads the same without it.

rules.name: Markup
rules.text: Markup languages reuse the categories: a heading or a list marker is a keyword, a quote a comment, inline code a string, a URL a link. Bold and italic keep the plain text color: their markers already show them.

rules.name: Code surfaces
rules.text: A block of code sits on the code surface, global.bg.code.surface: the Figma library's own token, aliasing the neutral subtle fill (global.bg.subtle.neutral.default). It is translucent, so a block stands out by the same amount on whatever surface level or sunken it sits on, and needs no level of its own. The colors are checked against the code surface and every line background, over every level and sunken.

rules.name: Marked lines
rules.text: An example can mark whole lines: highlighted (a line the author points out), inserted and deleted (lines an example adds or removes), error and warning. Each takes a background from the subtle fills (brand, success, error, warning), drawn over the code surface, and a marker that does not rest on color: a bar for a highlighted line, + and - for inserted and deleted lines, x and ! for errors and warnings. Every code color stays readable on every line background.

rules.name: Say why a line is marked
rules.text: A marker shows that a line is marked; the text around the example says why (what changed, what the error is). Markers are a visual aid, not the only place the information lives.

rules.name: Inline code and line numbers
rules.text: Code inside running text sits on the neutral subtle fill (global.bg.subtle.neutral.default), the fill the code surface aliases, and keeps the syntax colors' contrast rules. Line numbers, when a block shows them, use the tertiary on-base text color (global.text.on-base.neutral.tertiary). Neither needs a code token.

rules.name: Typography
rules.text: Code is set in the mono family (Typography foundation). Highlighting changes the color only: the text style stays the same for every category.

rules.name: Modes
rules.text: Every color has a value in every mode: the syntax categories take step 700 of each hue in light mode and the light steps (200 to 400) in dark mode; the code surface and the line backgrounds follow the subtle fills. One highlighting definition serves every mode: it names the categories, the mode picks the values.

rules.name: Languages
rules.text: The categories hold for any language. The mapping is written and checked for CSS, HTML, JavaScript, JSON, shell, YAML, diff and Markdown, the languages the documentation shows; a new language may need new scopes in the mapping, never a new color.

rules.name: Shiki theme
rules.text: pnpm tokens:build writes packages/tokens/dist/shiki-theme.json (@quantum-ds/tokens/shiki-theme.json) from the code tokens and the scope mapping in tokens.config.json (syntax): one theme in the TextMate format Shiki reads, whose colors are the CSS variables of the tokens, its editor background the code surface. It follows the mode of every data-theme context without a light and dark pair, and needs the design system's token CSS on the page. Marked lines come from Shiki's notation transformers ([!code highlight], [!code ++], [!code --], [!code error], [!code warning]); web/foundations/code.css, imported by web/index.css, draws them from the global.bg.code.* tokens with their default class names.

rules.name: Other platforms
rules.text: The code colors are semantic tokens: iOS and Android get them in their resolved trees for every mode, for a highlighter of their own to map its categories to.

specimens.name: Syntax colors
specimens.description: One color per syntax category, and the additions for diffs, invalid code and links, with the palette step each aliases in every mode.

specimens.name: Code backgrounds
specimens.description: The code surface and the backgrounds of marked lines, aliasing the subtle fills.

contrast.description: Keywords are text: on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Variables and properties, on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Function names, on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Class and type names, on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Strings, on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Numbers and constants, on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Comments are text people read, not decoration: same minimum as the rest of the code, on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Lines a diff adds. Text: on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Lines a diff removes. Text: on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Lines a context diff changes. Text: on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Invalid or deprecated code. Text: on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
URLs and links in code and markup. Text: on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
Plain code (identifiers, operators, punctuation) and the markers, on the code surface and every line background. Translucent: measured over every level and sunken.
The code surface against the level or sunken surface it sits on. Measured only: the text of the block, not its fill, carries the information.
The highlighted line background against the code surface it is drawn on, over every level and sunken. Measured only: the marker, not the tint, shows the state.
The inserted line background against the code surface it is drawn on, over every level and sunken. Measured only: the marker, not the tint, shows the state.
The deleted line background against the code surface it is drawn on, over every level and sunken. Measured only: the marker, not the tint, shows the state.
The error line background against the code surface it is drawn on, over every level and sunken. Measured only: the marker, not the tint, shows the state.
The warning line background against the code surface it is drawn on, over every level and sunken. Measured only: the marker, not the tint, shows the state.

guidelines.text: Every code color, comments, diff and link colors included, contrasts at least 4.5:1 with the code surface and with every line background, over every surface level and sunken, in every mode: code is text, whatever its category.
Color is not the only way to tell the categories apart: highlighting adds no information that the code text does not already carry, so a reader who cannot see the colors misses nothing.
A marked line never shows its state by color alone: a bar, + and -, x and ! mark it, and they survive forced colors mode, where the line backgrounds disappear.

Markers are generated content, which some assistive technologies do not announce. They carry alternative text (Added, Removed, Error, Warning) for those that do, and the text around an example says what its marked lines mean, so the information does not depend on the presentation.

In forced colors mode the browser replaces the color of every syntax category, and the background of the block, with system colors: the code stays readable, without highlighting. Nothing may depend on a syntax color surviving there.

examples.name: JavaScript
examples.description: A module with a class, private fields, a getter, regular expressions, template literals and async functions.

examples.name: CSS
examples.description: A product stylesheet: cascade layers, custom properties, functions, selectors, units and a media query.

examples.name: HTML
examples.description: A page using the Dropdown markup, with an embedded style sheet, a comment, an entity and a module script.

examples.name: JSON
examples.description: A DTCG token file: keys, strings, numbers, booleans and null.

examples.name: Shell
examples.description: A release script: variables, expansions, functions, conditions and loops.

examples.name: YAML
examples.description: A CI configuration: anchors, aliases, flow collections and multi-line lists.

examples.name: Marked lines
examples.description: A JavaScript module whose lines are marked: the old themes option is removed and replaced (- and +), the render call is highlighted, a call with an unknown language is an error, a call without a language a warning.

examples.name: Diff
examples.description: A context diff of the code colors: changed lines (!), an added line (+), a removed line (-), headers and ranges.

examples.name: Markdown
examples.description: A README: heading, quote, bold and italic, list, inline code, a link and a fenced JavaScript block.

examples.name: Invalid JSON
examples.description: A token file with two errors: a missing comma after keyword and an unquoted comment key, both marked invalid.

decisions.text: A block of code sits on global.bg.code.surface, the Figma library's code surface, which aliases the neutral subtle fill global.bg.subtle.neutral.default (light-switch base 400 at 10% in light mode, dark-switch base 400 at 10% in dark mode) instead of a surface level. The Shiki theme's editor background is the code surface. Marked lines draw their subtle fills over it.
decisions.rationale: Translucent, so a block of code stands out by the same amount on any surface level.

decisions.text: Every syntax color reaches 4.5:1 on the code surface and every line background, over every surface level and sunken, in every mode. The colors are the Figma library's own steps (light keyword lavender 700, class and type amber 800, string forest 700, number coral 700; dark keyword lavender 300, string forest 400), except the dark comment: dark-switch base 200 instead of the library's base 300, which reaches only 4.33:1 on the code surface over level 3. It is the only code color that diverges from the Figma library, to backport there.

Every syntax color reaches 4.5:1 on every surface level and sunken, in every mode, with the Figma library's own steps: since its POC2 export, light class and type is amber 800, string forest 700, number coral 700 and keyword lavender 700 (a new value, the lavender ramp now aliasing the purple tint), dark string forest 400, comment dark-switch base 300 and keyword lavender 300. No code color diverges from the library any more.
decisions.rationale: The library adopted passing steps for the four colors the previous decision had moved (one step further for class and type); keeping the repository's own steps would recreate a divergence for nothing.

decisions.text: The design system adds, from colors it already has: text colors global.text.code.inserted (light success 700, dark success 300), deleted and invalid (light error 600, dark error 200), changed (light severe 700, dark severe 300) and link (light brand 600, dark brand dark 200), mapped to diffs, invalid code and URLs; line backgrounds global.bg.code.highlighted, inserted, deleted, error and warning, aliasing the subtle brand, success, error, error and warning fills. Markup reuses the syntax categories. Marked lines also carry a marker (bar, +, -, x, !).

On the web, code is highlighted with Shiki, through one theme generated from the tokens (web/shiki-theme.json) whose colors are the CSS variables of the code tokens (var(--global-text-code-keyword)…). The same theme serves every mode; the documentation site uses it for every code block.

Every syntax color reaches 4.5:1 on every surface level and sunken, in every mode. Where the Figma library's step does not, the color takes the nearest step of the same hue that does: light class and type amber 700 (the Figma library 500), string forest 700 (600), number coral 700 (500); dark string forest 400 (500), comment dark-switch base 300 (400). Light mode is then step 700 of every hue and light-switch base 700 for comments; dark mode step 400 and dark-switch base 300.

Code syntax highlighting has seven semantic colors, the Figma library's code colors global.text.code: keyword (lavender), variable (orchid), function (azure), class and type (amber), string (forest), number (coral) and comment (neutral). Anything else in code keeps the primary on-base text color, global.text.on-base.neutral.primary.

changelog.note: Decisions code-surface and code-comment-dark (supersedes code-colors-library). The Figma library's export of 2026-11-23 (issue 68) adds global.bg.code.surface, aliasing the neutral subtle fill global.bg.subtle.neutral.default: light-switch base 400 #B5B5B5 at 10% in light mode, dark-switch base 400 #767676 at 10% in dark mode. A block of code sits on it instead of level 1: over level 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 / sunken it shows light #F6F6F6 / #F0F0F0 / #F6F6F6 / #F0F0F0 / #F0F0F0 (was level 1 #F7F7F7), dark #222222 / #2A2A2A / #303030 / #373737 / #1E1E1E (was level 1 #212121). The Shiki theme's editor background is the code surface. The contrast pairs measure the code colors on the code surface and every line background, laid over every level and sunken. Dark comment moves from dark-switch base 300 #9C9C9C to base 200 #B8B8B8: base 300 is 4.33:1 on the code surface over level 3, base 200 is 6.00:1 (a divergence from the Figma library, to backport). Contrast, lowest over every level, sunken and line background, the lines drawn over the code surface (4.5:1 required, WCAG 1.4.3): light keyword 8.07:1, variable 5.82:1, function 5.86:1, class and type 11.72:1, string 5.86:1, number 4.93:1, comment 7.71:1, inserted 7.02:1, deleted and invalid 5.46:1, changed 7.31:1, link 5.14:1, plain code 16.97:1; dark keyword 6.43:1, variable 5.05:1, function 5.36:1, class and type 6.55:1, string 5.05:1, number 4.82:1, comment 6.00:1, inserted 5.35:1, deleted and invalid 6.28:1, changed 4.83:1, link 8.64:1, plain code 7.64:1 (dark lowest over level 3). Measured only: the code surface against the area it sits on, light 1.06:1, dark 1.10 to 1.11:1; line backgrounds against the code surface, light 1.00 to 1.05:1, dark 1.07 to 1.53:1 (the markers carry the state, WCAG 1.4.1).

Decision code-colors-library (supersedes code-colors-contrast): the Figma library's POC2 export carries passing steps for every syntax color, so the code colors follow it again (Color foundation 3.1.0). Light: keyword #6B0DAC (lavender 700, new value), class and type #3B2D12 (amber 800, was 700 #7F6426), string #41661E (forest 700, new value), number #AC4836 (coral 700, new value); dark: keyword #D5AEFF (lavender 300, was 400), string #7BBA35 (forest 400, new value), number #FB826C, comment #9C9C9C (dark-switch base 300, unchanged step, new value). The link color aliases brand.palettes.core-colors (same values). Every code pair still passes 4.5:1 (pnpm validate).

Fix, no decision changed: the CSS and HTML samples (cards.css, dropdown.html) no longer load the component styles from @quantum-ds/components, which publishes the specs only; they load the component styles the product implemented from the specs.

Initial draft, decisions code-colors, code-colors-contrast, code-additions and shiki-theme. Owns the Figma library's global.text.code.* (keyword, variable, function, class-and-type, string, number, comment); five of them move to a passing step (light class-and-type, string, number; dark string, comment), the only divergences from the Figma library (pnpm tokens:figma-library). Adds, in tokens/additions/: global.text.code.inserted, deleted, changed, invalid, link, and the line backgrounds global.bg.code.highlighted, inserted, deleted, error, warning. New outputs web/shiki-theme.json (generated) and web/foundations/code.css (marked lines). Contrast, lowest over every surface level, sunken and line background, every platform (4.5:1 required, WCAG 1.4.3): light keyword 6.51:1, variable 5.82:1, function 5.85:1, class and type 4.90:1, string 6.43:1, number 5.67:1, comment 7.71:1, inserted 7.01:1, deleted and invalid 5.45:1, changed 7.31:1, link 5.16:1, plain code 17.00:1 (all lowest on the error line background); dark keyword 4.51:1, variable 5.59:1, function 5.94:1, class and type 7.25:1, string 5.78:1, number 5.73:1, comment 4.77:1, inserted 5.92:1, deleted and invalid 6.96:1, changed 5.35:1, link 9.61:1 (level 3), plain code 11.42:1. Measured only: line backgrounds against the level 1 block, light 1.03 to 1.05:1, dark 1.10 to 1.12:1 (the markers carry the state, WCAG 1.4.1).
